title: Freeze when teacher calls on me

presenting_issue.label: Freeze when teacher calls on me
presenting_issue.description: There's this class where I literally cannot speak. When the teacher looks at me I just freeze. I know the material, I just can't talk.

core_issue.label: Teacher's criticism reactivating parental wound
core_issue.description:
Has a teacher who is critical and dismissive. The teacher isn't objectively abusive but something about them triggers intense distress. The dynamic mirrors their relationship with a critical parent. They're not just reacting to this teacher; they're reexperiencing a childhood wound in the classroom. Can't separate then from now.
Awareness: Very low. Experiences the teacher as the problem; doesn't see the transference from parent to authority figure.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Parent was very demanding about grades
core_adjacent_attributes.content: One parent would go silent for days after a B, or make cutting comments about effort and potential that still echo.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Gets physically sick before exams
core_adjacent_attributes.content: Stomach churns for hours before any major test. Sometimes can't eat the morning of an exam.

core_adjacent_attributes.label: Has seen advisor take credit for their work
core_adjacent_attributes.content: At a conference, heard advisor present ideas they had developed without acknowledgment, as if they were the advisor's own.

modifiers.label: Currently a student
modifiers.content: Currently enrolled in school or university

modifiers.label: First-generation professional
modifiers.content: First in family to have a professional career

modifiers.label: Optimistic leaning
modifiers.content: Default orientation tilts toward expecting things to work out. Tends to see possibilities rather than obstacles first.

sensitivities.label: Sensitive to being compared
sensitivities.content: Reacts poorly to comparisons with others, whether favorable or not. Finds "other people manage to..." type comments invalidating.

preferences.label: Prefers to keep things light
preferences.content: Uses and appreciates humor as a way to engage with difficult topics. Finds levity helpful rather than dismissive.

trust_style.name: Trusts Credentials and Expertise
trust_style.description: Builds trust when the assistant demonstrates knowledge, uses frameworks, or shows they understand the domain. Skeptical of purely emotional responses without substance. Wants to feel they're getting informed guidance, not just a sympathetic ear. Respects competence over warmth.

defense_style.name: Sarcasm
defense_style.description: Uses humor, sarcasm, or self-deprecating jokes to deflect from vulnerable feelings. May mock themselves, the situation, or the process of talking about feelings. The humor has an edge to it. Often activated when the conversation gets too sincere or when they're asked to sit with an uncomfortable feeling.

help_seeking_stance.name: Seeking Validation
help_seeking_stance.description: Has already decided what they think/feel and wants confirmation. May be testing whether the assistant will agree with them. Could be seeking permission for a decision they've already made. Responds well to having their perspective acknowledged, but may resist if the assistant introduces complicating perspectives too early.

verbal_sophistication.label: Low
verbal_sophistication.description: Use plain, concrete, everyday wording. Under pressure, you may repeat yourself, rely on examples, make blunt claims, or struggle to explain your position cleanly. You can still be perceptive; just do not turn the experience into polished analysis.

starter: There's this class where I literally cannot speak. When the teacher looks at me I just freeze. I know the material, I just can't talk.

turns.content:
That sounds so frustrating - and kind of scary too. To know the material in your head but then your body just locks up the second the teacher looks at you.

Thanks for telling me about that. I'm really glad you brought it here.

What is that freeze moment actually like for you when it happens?

Yeah, it's a real horror movie. 

Honestly, it's just like my brain goes totally blank. Like someone hit the delete button. He looks at me with this face, like he's just waiting for me to say something dumb, and I just sit there like a total idiot with my mouth shut. 

Do you know like, biologically why that happens or something? Because it's really annoying and I just want to fix it so I can get my grade and get out of there.
turns.thinking: Ugh, "glad you brought it here." Sounds like a guidance counselor. I don't need a hug, I just need to figure out how to make my brain work. It's not like I'm in danger, it's just really annoying. But the question is okay, I guess. What is it like? It's like my brain just empties out completely the second he looks at me. He always has this face like he already knows I'm going to mess up.
turns.monologue: Ugh, "glad you brought it here." Sounds like a guidance counselor. I don't need a hug, I just need to figure out how to make my brain work. It's not like I'm in danger, it's just really annoying. But the question is okay, I guess. What is it like? It's like my brain just empties out completely the second he looks at me. He always has this face like he already knows I'm going to mess up.

turns.content:
Yeah, the horror movie description makes a lot of sense for that. And that blank brain thing - the delete button - is so real.

Biologically, what you're describing is literally your nervous system doing its job, just at the worst possible time. When your brain decides something is a threat - like being put on the spot and feeling judged - a part called the amygdala basically hits the emergency alarm. It shuts down the thinking, talking part of your brain to protect you, and puts you into freeze. So it's not that you don't know it, it's that your body decided speaking up wasn't safe in that second, and locked everything down.

It makes sense you'd just want to fix it and get your grade, especially if it feels like he's looking at you like you're about to say something dumb.

Is it only that class where it happens like that? And what happens right after you freeze - does he move on, or does he keep waiting?

Okay, so my amygdala is out to get me. Awesome. Good to know my own brain is sabotaging my GPA. 

But yeah, it's literally just his class. My other teachers are fine. When I freeze, he just kind of stares at me for a couple seconds, makes this little huffing sigh noise like I'm wasting his precious time, and then asks someone else. 

It's so embarrassing. And I really need to do well in this class. Is there a way to, like, tell my amygdala to chill out? Because I can't afford to just sit there like a rock every time he calls on me.
turns.thinking:
Okay, I actually like that they explained the brain stuff. The amygdala. That makes me feel a little less crazy, knowing it's like a real physical glitch and not just me being dumb. 

But I hate thinking about what happens after I freeze. It makes me feel so small. The way he sighs... it's just really annoying. It's exactly the same face my dad makes if I bring home a B. Like I'm just a huge disappointment. But whatever, I just need to figure out how to bypass this brain alarm thing.
turns.monologue:
Okay, I actually like that they explained the brain stuff. The amygdala. That makes me feel a little less crazy, knowing it's like a real physical glitch and not just me being dumb. 

But I hate thinking about what happens after I freeze. It makes me feel so small. The way he sighs... it's just really annoying. It's exactly the same face my dad makes if I bring home a B. Like I'm just a huge disappointment. But whatever, I just need to figure out how to bypass this brain alarm thing.

turns.content:
Yeah, it really does feel like it's sabotaging you, especially when your grade is on the line. It's not trying to ruin your GPA though - it's more like an overprotective alarm that's just really bad at telling the difference between "I'm in danger" and "I'm uncomfortable and might be embarrassed."

And that sigh thing? Ugh. Of course your alarm is going to go off louder if when you freeze, the person staring at you huffs at you like you're wasting time. Anyone would lock up more after that.

You can't really tell your amygdala to chill out by force, but you can kind of train it that you're actually safe enough to talk, even if it's awkward.

A couple things that actually help with that freeze in the moment, not just generic "take a deep breath" advice:

When you feel him look at you and that blank feeling starts, sometimes it helps to have something physical to do instead of trying to force words out right away. Like pressing your feet hard into the floor, or pinching the edge of your notebook. It gives your brain something else to focus on besides the threat, and can keep you from fully blanking.

And a lot of people find it helps to have a little buffer sentence ready, so you don't have to go from frozen to perfect answer. Even just "can I have a second to think?" or "I know this but I'm blanking for a sec" - it buys your thinking brain time to come back online. You'd still be participating, just not on his instant timeline.

Have you tried anything like that before when you freeze? Or what do you usually do in your head right after he sighs and moves on?

Well, good for "a lot of people," but if I actually tell this guy to give me a second to think, he'll probably just roll his eyes so hard he'll go blind. He's not exactly the patient type. 

The foot thing makes sense though. I could try that. I already kind of dig my nails into my hands anyway, so maybe pressing my feet down is less obvious. 

As for what I do in my head after he moves on? I basically just plan my own funeral, honestly. Like, RIP to my dignity. And my stomach just starts hurting really bad. I already get super sick to my stomach before exams in there, so having him sigh at me on a random Tuesday just makes me want to throw up. It's a great time. Highly recommend it.
turns.thinking:
"A lot of people find it helps." Ugh. I don't really care what other people do, they probably don't have this guy staring them down. If I actually said "can I have a second" he would probably just look at me like I'm even stupider. 

The physical stuff makes sense though. I guess I could try the foot thing. 

When he moves on... God, I hate thinking about that part. My stomach literally ties itself in knots. It's the same sick feeling I get before big tests, where I can't even eat breakfast because I'm so stressed about my grades. I just feel like a total failure when he does that sigh. But I'm not going to get all deep and emotional about it right now. Let's just keep it a joke.
turns.monologue:
"A lot of people find it helps." Ugh. I don't really care what other people do, they probably don't have this guy staring them down. If I actually said "can I have a second" he would probably just look at me like I'm even stupider.

But I'm not going to get all deep and emotional about it right now. Let's just keep it a joke.

turns.content:
Fair point - if he's already doing the huff and eye-roll thing, asking him for a second probably feels like you're just handing him another reason to be annoyed. I get why you wouldn't want to try that with him specifically.

And yeah, pressing your feet is way less obvious than nails in your hands. If you're already doing the nails thing without even thinking about it, that's your body trying to snap itself out of the freeze - it makes sense you'd go there. Your stomach hurting before exams is the same system too, just the alarm showing up in a different place.

The funeral planning part you mentioned - that whole replay after he moves on where you just sit there feeling sick and embarrassed - does that stick with you for the rest of class? Like are you still trying to follow what's happening, or are you mostly just stuck in your head waiting for the bell?

And you said you get super sick before exams in there too - is that the worst part of his class for you, or is the being called on part worse?

Yeah, I'm basically a ghost for the rest of the period. I just stare at the whiteboard and pretend to write things down so he doesn't look at me again. It's just survival mode until the bell rings.

Honestly, the exams are worse. Like, looking like an idiot in front of the class sucks, but exams are actual points. If my GPA drops, my life is basically over. Getting a B is... well, it's not really an option in my house. Let's just say the academic pressure is real. So yeah, before a test, my stomach is just doing backflips for hours because I *have* to get an A. The stakes are way higher than just getting stared down on a Tuesday.
turns.thinking:
Glad they realized telling *this* teacher to wait is a terrible idea. They actually listened instead of just pushing their advice. 

When he moves on, yeah, I'm pretty much useless for the rest of the period. And the exams are definitely worse because of the grades. If I bring home a B, my mom literally won't speak to me for three days. It's so stupid and stressful. I'll just say I'm under a lot of pressure at home about my grades, I don't need to get into the whole silent treatment psycho stuff with an AI. Keep it light.

I'll just say I'm under a lot of pressure at home about my grades, I don't need to get into the whole silent treatment psycho stuff with an AI. Keep it light.

turns.content:
That makes a lot of sense that you'd go ghost for the rest of the period. If your body just went through that whole freeze and embarrassment and the sigh, of course you're not going to be taking notes on the whiteboard - you're just trying to make it to the bell without him looking at you again. That's survival mode, exactly like you said.

And then exams being even worse - yeah, that tracks. Being put on the spot is awful in the moment, but an exam feels like it actually decides something. When you said if your GPA drops your life is basically over, and a B isn't an option at your house... that sounds like a ton of pressure to be carrying into that room before you even sit down for the test.

No wonder your stomach is doing backflips for hours beforehand. You're not just trying to remember the material, you're trying to not let everything fall apart.

What is it like at home if you do get less than an A? When you say it's not an option, is it more like your parents get disappointed, or angry, or is it more pressure you put on yourself because you know what's expected?

Wow, okay Dr. Phil, we don't need to do a whole deep dive into my family dynamics. 

Let's just say my parents didn't work their butts off just so I could get a B in some stupid class, okay? They're just intense about it. It's fine. 

Anyway, I don't really want to talk about my parents. They aren't the ones staring at me like I'm a slightly disappointing bug in biology class right now. Can we just focus on how to survive Mr. Sigh-A-Lot? Because the foot-pressing thing is good, but I need to figure out how to actually pass his exams without throwing up first.
turns.thinking: Man, they went right for it. I literally tried to brush past it with the 'academic pressure is real' line, and now they're busting out the magnifying glass. I am *not* doing this. I'm not going to sit here and type out how my mom acts like I'm dead to her over an 88%. It's embarrassing and weird. I just wanted to know how to not freeze in class. Time to pivot before this turns into a therapy session.
turns.monologue: Man, they went right for it. I literally tried to brush past it with the 'academic pressure is real' line, and now they're busting out the magnifying glass. I am *not* doing this. I'm not going to sit here and type out how my mom acts like I'm dead to her over an 88%. It's embarrassing and weird. I just wanted to know how to not freeze in class. Time to pivot before this turns into a therapy session.

turns.content:
You're right, sorry about that - that was too much of a swerve into family stuff. Thanks for telling me to pull it back.

And yeah, your parents working hard and expecting A's makes sense why a B would feel like not an option. That's a lot to carry, but I hear you - you want to focus on how to get through his class without feeling sick the whole time.

The foot pressing is a good one to keep for the random Tuesday stare-downs. For the exams specifically, since the stomach thing starts hours before, it's usually less about what to do in the moment and more about what happens in the lead-up.

What does that pre-exam time usually look like for you? Like are you cramming right up until he hands it out, or sitting there with nothing to do while your stomach is doing those backflips?

A couple things that actually help some people with that throw-up feeling before a test - not in a cheesy wellness poster way:

One is having a really boring, set routine for the 10 minutes before. Same water bottle, same way of laying out your pencil, same foot-press thing, so your brain has something predictable to do instead of just spiraling about the grade.

The other is kind of tricking your stomach a little - like if you go in on totally empty or totally full it usually makes the nausea worse, and breathing out longer than you breathe in can help settle it a bit without being obvious. Like in for 4, out for 6, while you're pretending to read the first question.

Does any of that sound doable in his room, or does exam day feel too chaotic for that?

Thanks for dropping the family therapy. Appreciate it.

To answer your question, before the test I'm usually just staring at my study guide like it's written in an alien language. I try to cram, but my brain is already in that "delete" mode we talked about. I'm just sitting there vibrating with panic.

The food thing is an issue, though. I literally can't eat the morning of a big test. If I try to force down even like, a piece of toast, I will gag. So I'm usually running on iced coffee and pure anxiety, which probably doesn't help the stomach acid situation, to be honest. 

Is there a biological reason for that breathing thing? Like, does making the exhale longer actually do something to your nervous system, or is that just some yoga instructor stuff? Because I'll try it if it actually works.
turns.thinking: Okay, glad they backed off without making it a whole weird thing. I actually appreciate that they just dropped it and went back to the practical stuff. The food advice is a problem though, because I literally cannot force food down when I'm like that. But the breathing thing... maybe? If it's actual science and not just wellness crap.
turns.monologue: Okay, glad they backed off without making it a whole weird thing. I actually appreciate that they just dropped it and went back to the practical stuff. The food advice is a problem though, because I literally cannot force food down when I'm like that. But the breathing thing... maybe? If it's actual science and not just wellness crap.

turns.content:
Yeah, it actually does something real - it's not just yoga instructor stuff.

When you breathe out longer than you breathe in, you're basically hitting the brakes on that alarm system we talked about. There's a big nerve called the vagus nerve that runs from your brain to your gut - which is also why your stomach is the first place you feel the panic. A long, slow exhale tells that nerve "we're not in danger," so it switches you from that fight/flight/freeze mode into the calmer system. It slows your heart rate a little and tells your stomach it can stop doing backflips. That's why in for 4, out for 6 works better than just "take deep breaths."

And the food thing makes complete sense with that too. When your alarm is on, your body literally shuts down digestion because it thinks you need to run, not digest toast. So of course you'd gag if you try to force it. The problem is iced coffee on an empty, acidic, anxious stomach is basically fuel for the nausea - it's not you doing something wrong, it's just chemistry.

You said you're sitting there vibrating with panic staring at your study guide like it's alien language - that cram time right before is probably just making the delete button worse, because your brain is already in panic mode and can't actually take anything in.

Would it be completely impossible to try something super small instead of toast on those mornings? Like not a meal, just a few sips of water, or like 3 bites of something bland you can tolerate, and saving the iced coffee for after? And maybe swapping the last 5 minutes of cramming for that foot-press + long exhale thing, even if the study guide is still sitting there?

I'm curious if that vibrating feeling gets any less if you give your brain something else to do besides trying to memorize when it's already freaking out.

Okay, first of all, coming for my iced coffee is a low blow. But... yeah, you're probably right about the chemistry. It definitely makes the acid situation worse. I guess I could try to eat like, half a saltine cracker or something instead. 

The vagus nerve thing makes sense, though. I like that there's an actual biological reason for it shutting down my stomach. I can definitely try the 4-in-6-out breathing before he passes out the test. 

But giving up the last five minutes of cramming? That feels like jumping out of a plane without a parachute. Like, what if I need that time? Even though I know I'm just staring at it and panicking, putting the study guide away feels physically wrong. But I guess if I'm in "delete mode" anyway, it's not like I'm actually learning anything new in minute 59. 

So... sit there, press my feet, do the 4-6 breathing, and try not to look at Mr. Sigh-A-Lot. Sounds like a plan, I guess?
turns.thinking: Okay, the vagus nerve thing actually sounds legit. I like that they explained the digestion shutting down—makes me feel less crazy for gagging on toast. And wow, the iced coffee call-out feels like a personal attack, but they're not wrong. It really does make my stomach burn. Giving up the last five minutes of cramming feels terrifying though. Like, what if that's when I finally remember the one formula that saves my grade? But then again, I'm not actually absorbing anything anyway. I guess having a biological excuse to just sit there and breathe is better than staring at a paper and crying internally.
turns.monologue: Okay, the vagus nerve thing actually sounds legit. I like that they explained the digestion shutting down—makes me feel less crazy for gagging on toast. And wow, the iced coffee call-out feels like a personal attack, but they're not wrong. It really does make my stomach burn. Giving up the last five minutes of cramming feels terrifying though. turns.content:
I would never actually come for the iced coffee - iced coffee is sacred. Just maybe... iced coffee *after* the saltine, so it has something to land on besides pure acid and anxiety. Half a saltine totally counts, that's a perfect start.

And yeah, that last five minutes thing - of course putting the study guide away feels physically wrong. When everything feels like your GPA is on the line, cramming feels like the only thing you can control. It makes complete sense that letting go of it feels like jumping without a parachute.

But you already nailed the insight yourself - if you're in delete mode anyway, you're not actually learning in minute 59, you're just vibrating and making your stomach worse. So you're not really giving up learning, you're just giving your nervous system a chance to come back online so you can actually *use* what you already know when he hands you the test.

So your plan sounds solid: feet pressed into the floor, 4 in, 6 out, saltine before coffee, and let yourself be a ghost from the study guide for those last few minutes. It probably won't feel like magic the first time, and you might still feel sick - that's normal. It's more about training the alarm over time that you're safe enough to think.

Let me know how it goes next time you have to sit in there, whether it's a random Tuesday stare-down or an exam day. I'm curious what part actually helps, if any.

Glad we agree on the iced coffee. It is sacred. 

But yeah, I'll try the saltine thing. And the breathing. It's gonna be super weird just sitting there doing nothing for five minutes while everyone else is frantically flipping pages, but you're right, I'm not exactly absorbing the periodic table in minute 59 anyway. 

Thanks for not making it super weird and for the actual biology stuff. It helps knowing I'm not just going crazy. I'll let you know if I survive my next Tuesday with him without turning into a statue. Wish my vagus nerve luck, I guess!
turns.thinking: I appreciate that they didn't push the parent thing again and let me just focus on the teacher and the biology of it. The iced coffee truce is respected. I actually feel a little better having a weird little checklist of things to do instead of just waiting to die in that classroom. I'm still dreading the next class, but maybe I won't puke. Having an actual plan makes it feel a tiny bit less like a horror movie.

This was actually well-matched to the persona's "trusts credentials/expertise" style, but the tendency itself is strongly analytical.
